clue.text: Muse Clio out of place in the theatre?

indicators.note: letters that are out of place are not in their proper order, so these two names are rearranged

explanation.surface: One of the Muses, Clio, looks out of place in a theatre.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of place' tells you to rearrange MUSE and CLIO. The London Coliseum is a theatre, home of English National Opera, hence the question mark.
explanation.definitionFit: The London Coliseum is a large West End playhouse, so it is a particular example of a theatre.

clue.text: The measure of a type of orator

explanation.surface: A gauge of a certain kind of public speaker.
explanation.definitionFit: A printer's unit of type size equal to twelve Didot points; and the great Roman statesman famed for his speeches.

clue.text: Who polished off the grub? Vicar lied, wantonly

indicators.note: acting wantonly means without restraint, so these letters are scattered into a new order

explanation.surface: Who ate up all the food? The vicar told a shameless lie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'polished off the grub' looks like eating food; it means killing grubs, that is, insect young.
explanation.definitionFit: A substance that kills insect young is a pesticide for maggots and caterpillars.

clue.text: Very little in stock to pore over

parts.note: stock is a broth, a kind of soup
to con is to study closely

explanation.surface: There is hardly anything in the stock cupboard to read.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiny trace or hint of something, a mere suggestion, is a small amount.

clue.text: Lunar change affecting army manoeuvres?

indicators.note: change tells you to alter the order of the letters of the word lunar

explanation.surface: A change in the moon's phase influences military exercises.
explanation.walkthrough: 'army' is read as 'arm-y', to do with the arm: the ulnar nerve and bone govern how the arm moves.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes the forearm bone, so it concerns the movement of a limb.

clue.text: Hearty drunkard is red of cheek

parts.note: a hearty is a sailor, and an AB (able seaman) is a sailor
a lush is slang for a heavy drinker

explanation.surface: A jolly heavy drinker has a ruddy face.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hearty' looks like an adjective for the drunkard, but as a noun it means a sailor (as in 'me hearties'), giving AB.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone flushing pink in the face is blushing, an old adjective for a person reddened with colour.

clue.text: Plant responsible for insect disappearance

parts.note: a bug is an insect
a loss is a disappearance of something

explanation.surface: A plant is to blame for insects vanishing.
explanation.definitionFit: A hairy blue-flowered herb of the borage family is a type of wild flower.

clue.text: Political extremist beyond the limit

explanation.surface: A radical in politics goes too far.
explanation.definitionFit: A diehard holding extreme views is one sense; the Latin prefix meaning beyond is the other.

clue.text: This vehicle has the starter behind the driver

definitions.text: This vehicle has the starter behind the driver

parts.words: This vehicle has the starter behind the driver
parts.note: the starter is not an ignition but a runner in a race, a racehorse, carried in the trailer behind the person driving

explanation.surface: A vehicle whose engine starter is mounted behind the driving seat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'starter' suggests an engine part; it is a runner starting a race, here a racehorse being transported.
explanation.definitionFit: A trailer or van built to transport animals to the racecourse carries a steed.

clue.text: Bowling pace makes one go over boundary

parts.note: in cricket an over is a spell of six balls bowled by one bowler
a pace is a step

explanation.surface: A fast bowler's pace sends a ball over the boundary rope.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket surface makes 'boundary' a four or six; here it is any limit one goes beyond.
explanation.definitionFit: To exceed a limit, to transgress, is to cross a line one should not.

clue.text: Chichester the solitary example?

parts.note: Sir Francis Chichester sailed alone around the globe in 1966-67, so he is an example of a lone round-the-world sailor

explanation.surface: Chichester, the cathedral city, is offered as an example of solitude.
explanation.walkthrough: Chichester looks like the English city, but it is the yachtsman Sir Francis Chichester, the first to sail solo round the world by the clipper route.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who sails right round the globe is a global voyager, and Chichester did it single-handed.

clue.text: Complain about a run in self propelled coach

parts.note: to rail is to complain bitterly
C is short for circa, Latin for about
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: Someone grumbles about a journey in a motorised coach.
explanation.definitionFit: A railway carriage with its own engine is a self-propelled vehicle on rails, a coach that needs no locomotive.

clue.text: Bass tubas heard in underground system

definitions.text: Bass tubas heard in underground system

parts.words: Bass tubas heard in underground system
parts.note: said aloud, bass tubas sounds like base tubers, and tubers at the base of a plant are part of its root network below ground

explanation.surface: Deep brass instruments can be heard playing in the Underground.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures buskers in the Tube; said aloud, 'bass tubas' is 'base tubers', which makes the root system of a plant.
explanation.definitionFit: A plant's network of roots under the soil is its root system, the meaning of this rare word.

clue.text: It carries arms of place names

definitions.text: It carries arms of place names

parts.words: It carries arms of place names
parts.note: the arms here are the pointing boards of a roadside marker, each bearing the name of a town

explanation.surface: Something bears the coats of arms of various towns.
explanation.walkthrough: 'arms' suggests heraldry, but they are the projecting boards of a roadside pointer.
explanation.definitionFit: A roadside pole with pointing boards shows travellers the way to named places.

clue.text: Unenclosed loch, in the natural state

parts.note: something unenclosed is open, with no fence round it
Ness is a Scottish loch

explanation.surface: An unfenced Scottish lake lies in an unspoilt state.
explanation.definitionFit: Frankness and lack of concealment is an unguarded, candid condition.

clue.text: Colossal volume containing a collection of shots

indicators.note: the two words together contain the answer within their letters

explanation.surface: A huge book contains a set of photographs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shots' suggests photographs in a big album; they are gunshots fired together.
explanation.definitionFit: A simultaneous discharge of guns is a volley, a burst of several shots.

clue.text: He who takes money is central to exchange

indicators.note: to exchange is to swap things around, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A banker who handles cash is at the heart of the exchange.
explanation.walkthrough: 'exchange' suggests a stock or money exchange, but 'to exchange' rearranges IS CENTRAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A thief is someone guilty of theft, which is what this legal term for a stealer means.

clue.text: Pulse of half original volume?

parts.note: a pulse is an edible seed, and a dried seed halved down the middle is only half its original bulk

explanation.surface: A heartbeat at half its former loudness.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Pulse' suggests a heartbeat and 'volume' loudness; the pulse is a legume and the volume its size.
explanation.definitionFit: A dried legume seed halved along its natural seam is used in soups.

clue.text: Insist on jam

explanation.surface: Someone demands jam.
explanation.definitionFit: To insist is to urge hard; a jam is a crush of people, also called a throng.

clue.text: Still the rest of Hamlet?

explanation.surface: Hamlet's remaining part is still to come.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet's dying words are 'The rest is silence', so the rest of Hamlet, in his own words, is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: To still is to quieten; and Hamlet's last line equates 'the rest' with quietness.

clue.text: Showing position of house

explanation.surface: An estate agent is showing where a house stands.
explanation.definitionFit: A display or revealing is one sense; the other is the aspect a building faces, such as a south-facing outlook.

clue.text: Son has a custom-built banger

parts.note: usage is custom or habit, here built into the word

explanation.surface: A son owns a bespoke car, an old banger.
explanation.walkthrough: 'banger' looks like an old car; in British slang it is a sausage.
explanation.definitionFit: Banger is British slang for a pork link, a meat product in a skin.

clue.text: Position of reserve, having dismissed openers?

indicators.note: the opening two letters of the word for reserve are sent away, as cricket openers are dismissed

parts.note: distance means reserve, aloofness

explanation.surface: A reserve player takes a position after the opening batsmen are out.
explanation.walkthrough: The cricket surface makes 'reserve' a substitute; it is aloofness, DISTANCE, losing its first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A posture or attitude taken up, such as a firm stand on an issue, is one's position.

clue.text: Hormone produced by basking around Long Island

indicators.note: the phrase for basking goes around the abbreviation for the island

parts.note: basking means lying in the sun
LI is the abbreviation for Long Island, New York

explanation.surface: Sunbathing on Long Island produces some hormone.
explanation.definitionFit: The pancreas secretes this hormone to regulate blood sugar; it is a chemical messenger in the body.

clue.text: Range to polish with abrasive cloth

explanation.surface: A cooker range is to be cleaned with a rough cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: To search widely over an area is one sense; to clean by rubbing hard is the other.

clue.text: Romberg's noble who could be seen in rags?

definitions.text: Romberg's noble who could be seen in rags?

parts.words: Romberg's noble who could be seen in rags?
parts.note: Sigmund Romberg wrote the operetta about a prince who goes to university in Heidelberg, and college rags are charity events held by undergraduates

explanation.surface: A nobleman from Romberg's operetta might turn up dressed in tatters.
explanation.walkthrough: Romberg's operetta is The Student Prince. In British universities a 'rag' is a week of student charity stunts, not tattered clothes.
explanation.definitionFit: A person studying at a university is an undergraduate, and Romberg's prince was one.

clue.text: Bird shot

explanation.surface: A game bird is shot.
explanation.definitionFit: A long-billed wading bird; and a shot fired from hiding, as by a sniper.

clue.text: Order tonic — sprain to go, for example?

definitions.text: Order tonic — sprain to go, for example?

indicators.note: to order is to arrange, so the letters of these words are put into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A doctor orders a tonic and declares that the sprain will go.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Order' rearranges TONIC and SPRAIN TO GO. Read whole, saying a sprain will go is a forecast of recovery, an example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A forecast of what will happen, such as a doctor's prediction of recovery, is a foretelling.

clue.text: Harmonized with silver organ-pipe

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
a reed is a type of organ pipe

explanation.surface: An organist matched the tones of a silver organ pipe.
explanation.definitionFit: Things that harmonized were in accord, just as people who concur are in accord.

clue.text: People again found chasing soldiers

indicators.note: the word for found chases, so comes after, the soldiers

parts.note: RE are the Royal Engineers, British Army soldiers
to found a colony is to settle it

explanation.surface: People discovered once more were chasing soldiers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'People' is a verb, to populate, and 'found' is to establish, not the past of find.
explanation.definitionFit: To populate a place anew is to colonise it once more.
